content: Most infant deaths associated with chronic lung disease (CLD) are attributed to respiratory failure, persistent pulmonary artery hypertension (PAH) with cor pulmonale, or infections. While the exact prevalence of PAH in infants with CLD remains unclear, it is well-documented that infants with CLD and severe PAH face a significantly high mortality rate. Currently, aside from oxygen supplementation, no specific therapeutic interventions have been definitively established as effective for managing PAH in premature infants with CLD. The clinical efficacy of vasodilators in this population remains largely unproven, and there are ongoing concerns regarding their potential adverse effects. The objective of this review was to evaluate the existing evidence regarding the benefits and risks of hydralazine therapy in infants with persistent hypoxemic respiratory failure. To achieve this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE via PubMed, EMBASE, and other clinical trial registries, up to November 2011. The search strategy employed a combination of the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's highly sensitive search methods for identifying randomized trials, along with specific MeSH terms and free-text keywords such as hydralazine, vasodilator agent, antihypertensive agent, heart diseases, lung diseases, respiratory tract diseases, infant, and randomised controlled trial. The inclusion criteria for this review were limited to randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and quasi-randomized trials involving low birth weight (LBW) infants with persistent hypoxemic respiratory failure who received any form of hydralazine therapy. Two independent reviewers assessed the quality of the trials based on pre-specified criteria. The review did not identify any studies that met the inclusion criteria. Consequently, there is insufficient evidence to determine the safety and efficacy of hydralazine in LBW infants with persistent hypoxemic respiratory failure. Given that hydralazine is both inexpensive and potentially beneficial, the authors recommend conducting randomized controlled trials to explore its utility in this population. Such trials are particularly important in clinical settings where alternative therapies, such as sildenafil, inhaled nitric oxide (iNO), or extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO), are unavailable.
